Wednesday | AI, Enterprise & Leadership

Controls always arrive. They just arrive late, and they arrive as a bill. I have built AI companies since the 1990s and watched that sequence run three separate times. Capability ships first and gets the applause. Accountability ships second and gets the budget fight. Three things landed in three days this week, and all three were about the second half.

1. OWASP published version 2.01 of its State of Agentic AI Security and Governance. The taxonomy is not the story. The story is that almost every threat the first edition described as plausible now has a CVE, a vendor advisory, or a production incident attached to it. The new edition adds a live incidents tracker, agent identity, AI bills of materials, supply chain provenance, and a map of 42 regulatory instruments across ten jurisdictions.

2. @Anaconda acquired Enkrypt AI, folding pre-deployment red teaming, runtime guardrails and compliance automation into its platform. The compliance piece is the tell. It maps frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and HIPAA into enforceable controls. Not guidance. Controls.

3. Five teams on rust-lang/rust adopted an LLM policy. Models may assist. Contributors must disclose. Reviewers may close what does not comply. The maintainers named the cause plainly: a surge in low-effort machine-generated contributions.

What this rhymes with: open source was consumed freely for twenty years. Then SolarWinds and Log4Shell happened, and software bills of materials went from good practice to procurement requirement inside eighteen months. The code did not get better. The accountability got named.

Second-order effect: agent governance stops being a policy document and becomes a purchasing line item. Whoever owns the runtime guardrail owns the audit trail.

For leaders: you cannot delegate accountability for an agent to the team that deployed it. Ask who signs the incident report before you ask what the agent can do.

You are not behind. You are unarmed.

— Rob Frasca | COSIMO Digital | cosimodigital.com
Capital markets, rebuilt on-chain, amplified by AI

#AIGovernance #EnterpriseAI #Leadership

posts.title: Copyright Law is Catching Up to Suno in Germany.
posts.author: Tito Tahan
posts.snippet:
Copyright Law is Catching Up to Suno in Germany.

I just read a German court has ruled that Suno infringed copyrights represented by GEMA, ordering the AI music company to disclose profits connected to the infringement and pay damages, with the amount still to be determined. The decision can be appealed, but it marks one of the first significant court victories against a generative AI music platform in Europe.

For signed musicians, the ruling strengthens the argument that copyrighted recordings cannot simply become AI training material without consequences.

Independent musicians should recognize that ownership documentation is becoming more valuable as courts begin recognizing the commercial importance of training data.

Producers now have another reason to protect every contribution. A recording may generate value not only through streaming, but through future AI licensing markets.

Record labels gain stronger negotiating leverage as courts begin validating the commercial importance of licensed training data.

Rights holders should focus on the bigger pattern. The conversation is shifting from whether AI should pay, for how AI should pay.

Here is my insight. Every new technology eventually reaches the same point. Innovation meets ownership. The companies that survive are usually the ones that adapt their business model to intellectual property, not around it. That is where long-term value is created.

Treat your catalog like strategic infrastructure. Keep your registrations current. Strengthen your metadata. Preserve your contracts. The companies with the cleanest rights will be in the strongest position when AI licensing becomes standardized. Because the next generation of music revenue may depend less on how often your songs are played and more on how they are legally permitted to be learned from.

If courts continue ruling that AI training requires permission, will licensing become the foundation of the AI music economy instead of litigation?
posts.reason: Substantive discussion of copyright, AI training data, and IP rights with German court decision—highly relevant to their tech law practice and invites expert perspective.

comments.text: Worth flagging the distinction the post glosses over: a GEMA-style ruling establishes infringement liability for training on protected works, but it says nothing about licensing becoming mandatory or standardised - those are two very different regulatory outcomes and only one of them is before a court right now.

Given the case is still open on appeal and damages aren't quantified, what would actually change in your view if the appellate court narrows the finding to specific tracks rather than the training corpus as a whole?

We advise clients on IP assignment and rights documentation for tech products, and the same lesson applies here as with any licensing dispute: clean, current registrations and contracts are worth far more at the point of a claim than at the point of negotiation - by then it's too late to fix gaps in the chain of title.

Crypto exchanges were built around a simple advantage: markets that never close. Today, platforms are extending that model beyond Bitcoin and altcoins into tokenized stocks, funds, and derivatives linked to global companies.

posts.author: Mariano Olivera

#CLARITY #ACT #UPDATE

President Trump just announced to hold the last negotiations meeting today to pass the Crypto Clarity Act.

Democrats are now supporting the bill.

Final negotiations on the Crypto Clarity Act are scheduled for today in Washington, D.C — but the US Senate schedule does not include a ClarityAct vote for today.

■ It's very important to understand what the Clarity Act unlocks:

Passing the Senate this week → still not law.
Becoming law (enactment) → still not fully operational.
Fully operational framework → roughly 9 to 12+ months after it is signed into law.

Enactment ≠ passage.

Most of the important operational pieces have delayed effective dates 60, 180, & 360 days after enactment — because Federal Agencies have to write the actual rules.

Many core titles (especially the main market-structure & classification pieces) take effect 360 days after the date of enactment...

Some intermediary / registration-related pieces take effect 270 days after enactment.

The Agencies, so the Security Exchange Commission & U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, are required to write detailed rules after the Clarity Act passes ► the provision becomes effective either on:

The general delayed date (270 or 360 days), OR 60 days after the final rule is published in the Federal Register.

Also important to note that US institutional capital is around $70 Trillion (including retirement plans ~$45-50 Trillion, pensions, insurance companies, mutual funds, endowments & other managed capital) — with only 0.2% of that being currently in crypto.

But, even with the Clarity Act passing, it's not like we will get anywhere near $50 Trillion in buying orders for Bitcoin right away...

First because of what I just shared, the SEC & CFTC need to put the rules in writting, that can happen as fast as 60 days or as long as 360 days.

Second, because even after regulatory clarity, the typical path is a 1–3% maximum allocation for most retirement/pension/insurance/mutual fund/endowment/etc plans.

This will happen gradually. It's not a sudden flood.

That said, just a 1% shift of $70 Trillion is $700Bn.

This is MASSIVE relative to current Bitcoin market structure — but the speed & the price impact depend on how & when that capital actually arrives, not just the existence of the legal green light...

Furthermore, the real variables that decide whether we get the faster hybrid advance (more like past retail-led cycles) or stay in the slower controlled mode are US fiscal liquidity expansion & the behavior of real yields + the dollar's strength.

IF those 2 cooperate with Clarity, the path can include a faster reprice to ATH at $125k for BTC, then a move to $180k in my opinion, followed by a bear market for a few months, then up again. 

If they do not, the market remains in the slow institutional accumulation style like what we saw from $15k to $125k.

Will we see the upper bands of the Bitcoin Rainbow Chart being explored this time or not? 🌈

posts.title: I recently spoke with Marina D'Angelo about her work with prediction-market founders, and it felt like the perfect way to kick off a new LinkedIn series: Prediction People.
posts.author: Stuart Crowley
posts.snippet:
I recently spoke with Marina D'Angelo about her work with prediction-market founders, and it felt like the perfect way to kick off a new LinkedIn series: Prediction People.

I want to meet more of the people doing the actual work, and understand what they’re seeing from inside the category.

Marina is Head of Europe at DLT LAW.

Here’s our first Prediction People Q&A.

Q: What first drew you and DLT Law into prediction markets?

“It started with a random conversation with my husband a few years ago about, of all things, a prediction market on the weather in Norway.”

Oddly specific, but it stuck. Once Marina pulled the thread, she found a category sitting at the intersection of traditional finance, betting, and crypto, which is exactly where much of her career has lived.

Q: Where do you begin when a founder wants to launch?

“Tell me everything about what you built. Literally, take me on a journey.”

Before discussing licences or jurisdictions, Marina wants the product in full colour: what happens when a user taps the button, what appears on screen, what’s happening in the backend, and who’s doing what.

The founder tells the story and she steers the conversation. No interrogation or legal lecture.

Q: What do prediction-market founders most often misunderstand?

The most common assumption Marina hears is: “Surely this falls outside of regulation.”

Another is: “An offshore gambling licence solves it.”

There’s also the financial-instrument blind spot. Some founders see gambling as the end of the analysis and don’t consider whether the product might fall into another regulatory category.

The less glamorous legal basics can be just as costly, including founder agreements, client terms, and where the company is incorporated.

Q: What does an offshore gambling licence actually cover?

Marina describes it as “permission from one regulator, in one jurisdiction, to operate a gambling product.”

It may help establish credibility with counterparties. It doesn’t automatically cover where users live, banking and payment rails, advertising rules or how another regulator might classify the product.

“Credibility isn’t the same as coverage.”

Q: What separates serious builders from companies following the momentum?

For Marina, it isn’t about arriving early. Later entrants can be every bit as serious. What matters is whether they know the product inside out, can explain what they’ve built and why, and recognise where their expertise ends.

As she puts it: “Serious builders know exactly where their own expertise ends, and they plug in the right support, legal or otherwise, rather than pretending those gaps don’t exist.”

That feels like a very good place to begin Prediction People.

If you work in prediction markets and would like to be featured in a future Q&A, DM me.

I’d love to hear what you’re building, what you’re learning and what you think the category is missing.

posts.title: What's your diagnosis?
posts.author: Hassan Akram
posts.snippet:
What's your diagnosis? 


Everyone obsesses over getting stronger.


Almost nobody asks whether they’re solving the right problem.
That mistake costs offers.


Three examples.
If you’re applying for investment banking, you might think your issue is commercial awareness.


It often isn’t.
The problem is commercial fluency.


Can you explain why tariffs matter to an M&A deal?
Can you connect interest rates to leveraged finance?


Can you explain how geopolitical volatility changes a CEO’s acquisition strategy?


Recruiters aren’t testing whether you read the Financial Times.
They’re testing whether you think like someone already sitting in the room.


If you’re applying for private equity, you might think your issue is technical knowledge.


It often isn’t.
The problem is judgement.
Can you identify the real value creation opportunity?


Can you separate operational improvement from financial engineering?
Can you explain why one business deserves capital while another doesn’t?
The strongest candidates don’t necessarily know more.


They prioritise better.
If you’re applying for venture capital, you might think your problem is networking.
It often isn’t.


The problem is pattern recognition.
Can you explain why this founder wins?
Why this market is changing?
Why this product scales?


Why this company becomes venture-backed while another never raises?
VC is fundamentally a business of judgement under uncertainty.
Your thinking should reflect that.


The same principle applies everywhere.
Many candidates think:
“I need better interview answers.”
The real issue is often that their communication lacks conviction.
Or structure.


Or executive presence.
Or vocal control.
Others think:


“My CV isn’t good enough.”
The real issue is that they’ve listed experiences…
…without building a compelling investment case around them.
Others think:


“I just need more experience.”
The real issue is that they haven’t translated the experience they already have into evidence recruiters can recognise in seconds.


This is why elite recruitment is so difficult.
Applications measure one thing.
Psychometric tests measure another.


Interviews assess something different.
Assessment centres test something else entirely.
Every stage is another judgement gate.


Every stage asks a different question.
Treating them all as the same problem is one of the biggest mistakes candidates make.


The candidates who consistently secure offers rarely have perfect CVs.
They’ve simply diagnosed the real constraint earlier than everyone else.
Once you identify the bottleneck…


…the solution usually becomes much clearer.


That’s how many of the families we advise have gone on to secure offers across elite corporate law, investment banking, private equity, venture capital and consulting

Not because they suddenly became smarter.

Because they stopped solving the wrong problem.


Diagnosis comes before preparation.
Everything else follows.

posts.title: Bliss Abode Pvt. Ltd. and Bliss House Pvt. Ltd. had secured significant credit facilities from Indiabulls Housing Finance, backed by personal guarantees furnished by Rana Kapoor an
posts.author: Filfox Law Group
posts.snippet:
Bliss Abode Pvt. Ltd. and Bliss House Pvt. Ltd. had secured significant credit facilities from Indiabulls Housing Finance, backed by personal guarantees furnished by Rana Kapoor and his wife, Bindu Kapoor.After Kapoor's 2020 arrest, Indiabulls invoked a clause allowing it to recall the loan if the borrower's ability to repay was seriously affected, and demanded immediate repayment. The companies defaulted. The dispute went to arbitration and in 2023 the arbitrator ruled in the lender's favour. Bindu Kapoor challenged this ruling in the Delhi High Court under Section 34.

Meanwhile, the debt was sold to JC Flowers ARC, which approached the NCLT to start insolvency proceedings against the two companies under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). 

Issues
Can a company be pushed into insolvency while the arbitral award against it is still being contested in court?

Can loan recall notices be challenged years after they were issued, having gone unquestioned at the time?

Does the "default "stand on its own, separate from the arbitral award?

The Supreme Court ruled against Bindu Kapoor. It held that she never challenged the 2020 recall notices when they were issued, so she couldn't question them now, years later. More importantly, the Court noted that not a single rupee had been repaid since 2020  a continuing default too serious to overlook. 
It clarified that simply filing a Section 34 challenge doesn't freeze or cancel the debt unless a court specifically grants a stay no such stay existed here. The insolvency plea was based on this ongoing non-payment, not solely on the arbitral award. 

The judgment reinforces that a pending challenge to an arbitral award, in the absence of a stay, does not impede insolvency proceedings under the IBC. It strengthens creditor rights by affirming that continuing financial default remains a valid and independent basis for initiating insolvency proceedings.

posts.title: £8 million. 502 people.
posts.author: Crypto Accountants
posts.snippet:
£8 million. 502 people. 
And that's just the ones who came forward voluntarily.

HMRC has collected over £8m from crypto investors since 2024, all through voluntary disclosures. 

Alongside those 502 settlements, HMRC sent "nudge letters" to roughly 100,000 people it suspected of underpaying tax on crypto gains.

This isn't HMRC waiting for people to confess anymore. 
It's HMRC already knowing whom to ask.

The UK adopted the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) on 1 January this year. 

Every UK exchange, wallet provider, and broker now has to collect ID details, tax residency, and full transaction histories on their users and hand them to HMRC annually. 

That data then gets shared with 76 other countries on the same standard, with first exchanges due in 2027.

The pressure is showing up on both sides:

➝ 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝘀 face fines of £300 per user record for missing or inaccurate reports, plus the risk of losing their spot on the FCA's Cryptoasset Register.
➝ 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 are settling for more. Average settlements jumped from £12,654 in 2024/25 to £21,552 this past year, as the reporting net widens and old unreported gains become harder to hide.

Quick refresher if you hold crypto or advise someone who does:

➡ Selling, swapping, spending, or gifting crypto can all trigger Capital Gains Tax.
➡ The CGT-free allowance is just £3,000 a year. Gains above that are taxed at 18% or 24% depending on income.
➡ Frequent trading doesn't automatically make you a "trader." Most crypto activity is still treated as investment (CGT), not a business (Income Tax).
➡ Reporting is on you, usually via Self-Assessment. "The exchange didn't send a tax form" isn't a defence.

If you have unreported crypto activity, voluntary disclosure still beats waiting for the letter. 

The data's on its way to HMRC either way.

Principles are important. Compromising your principles erodes them. However, it’s more than possible to make every issue one of principles.

When people start trimming off the edges of life of others to benefit themselves, they are capable of making up all kinds of reasons, even ones that seem compassionate or logical and (non) confirming them in law.

The dilemma always was & is that, either help more lives, or save yourself?

Job scams generally involve fraudsters using any platform's to advertise fraudulent job roles. Scammers exploit users looking for employment advice or job leads by funnelling them away from the platform into gaining financial benefits.

Don’t Compromise - people are involved, you have to consider their rights, feelings, and circumstances first. No one should infringe or violate against another, is first & foremost. There’s nothing to compromise. Quit what you’re doing.

There are two ways to achieve success in your life - Merit and performance or Crime and immorality.  In every society, both type of people exist.

If you are extremely talented & hardworking, you can achieve success in life without compromising on your ethics & morality. If you don’t have merit, the only way to succeed is by engaging in crime, corruption & immorality because the honest & meritorious people don’t venture into these fields and you have lesser competition here.

A person should never be punished for a minor mistake or flaw. But, Punishment should always be for:

-To teach the person and help them grow and fit into their society. Specifically, to teach them that certain behaviors are not acceptable.

-To balance a wrong that this person inflicted on another. 'Balancing’ has been at the root of many justice systems throughout history. It's an effective way to redress bad actions.

-To remove a person who is a threat to people or society and has been resistant to lesser forms of correction. Society does have the right to protect itself from incorrigible people who have shown their belief that their own wants are more important to them than the safety and security of those around them. 

Punishment should always be for the betterment of the individual or of society. It should never be used simply to cause pain.

The most dangerous thing in tech right now is not AI.
It's people who refuse to understand it.

We are living through the most significant technological shift in human history. Every single industry — healthcare, finance, education, agriculture, law — is being quietly rewritten by artificial intelligence. Not in the future. Right now. Today.
And yet, most people are still watching from the sidelines.

Here's the uncomfortable truth about AI in 2026:

— AI will not replace you. But someone who knows how to use AI better than you absolutely will. The gap between those who adapt and those who don't is widening every single month.

— The biggest breakthroughs are not happening in Silicon Valley alone. They are happening in small teams, startups, and individual developers who decided to stop fearing the technology and started building with it instead.

— Ethical AI is not optional anymore. As these systems make decisions that affect real human lives — hiring, lending, healthcare, justice — the responsibility to build them responsibly falls on every single engineer, designer, and product manager in the room.

— Curiosity is the new competitive advantage. Not your degree. Not your years of experience. The developers winning right now are the ones asking better questions, experimenting faster, and staying uncomfortable on purpose.

We are not in an AI bubble. We are at the beginning of an era that will define the next 50 years of human progress.

The question is not whether AI will change your field. It already has.
The question is: what are you building with it?
Start today. Stay curious. Think human.

When I decided to step out and take my father’s kunafa legacy to the world, people looked at me and only saw my roles.

They saw a housewife. A mother. A daughter-in-law.

And they asked me questions—sometimes out of concern, sometimes out of doubt: "How can a woman handle a street food startup? How will you deal with male vendors late at night? How will you manage packaging, production, and angry customers?"

What they forgot is the quiet strength every woman carries inside. A woman gives birth, brings life into this world, and holds whole families together through every storm. If we can do that, we can do anything.

I knew in my heart I wanted to make my father’s legacy reach the sky. But I also knew I couldn't do it alone. God blessed me with a team that believed in me: my husband and my father stood right beside me, handling the heavy ground operations and vendor battles so I could lead, design, and build this brand.

Our journey started as a humble stall on Burns Road. But very soon, city (KMC) issues forced us to shut down. My heart broke into pieces. Most people told us to give up. But the love of our customers kept us going. We moved to our home kitchen, working day and night doing deliveries and pickups, saving every bit of strength and money for our next chance.

Today, with tears in my eyes and pride in my heart, I am sharing our biggest news: We have officially rented and opened our own physical shop on Burns Road!

It is not a big dream showroom yet. It is simple, humble, and a work in progress. But it exists, it is ours, and it stands as a proud, women-owned brand right in the culinary heart of Karachi.

To my corporate network, mentors, and friends: I’m sharing this not to advertise a product, but to share a real story of womanhood, family love, and refusing to give up.

Please follow our journey. 
Visit us on Burns Road, try our kunafa, and guide me on how I can do better. Whether it’s packaging, service, or strategy—I want to learn from you all.

Thank you to everyone who held our hands when we had nothing but a small stall. Here’s to women who dare to dream, and the families who lift them up! 💖🚀

posts.title: Your TA tech stack isn't the reason global hiring stalls. Your compliance blind spot is.
posts.author: Employmint
posts.snippet:
Your TA tech stack isn't the reason global hiring stalls. Your compliance blind spot is. 

Every CHRO we talk to has the same 2026 mandate: hire faster, hire globally, hire smarter. But almost none of them have a compliance model that can keep up. 

Here's what the data says:
- More than 40% of global companies reported at least one compliance failure last year that led to fines, penalties or back pay; and worker misclassification was a leading cause
- The average compliance failures costs organizations around $42,000 per incident, before you count reputational damage or the deal it kills
- 57% payroll and HR leaders name local compliance as their single biggest challenge this year. Yet 42% of organizations still have no formalized global hiring or payroll strategy
- Nearly 6 in 10 UK HR leaders now expect most new hires to sit outside their home country

Cross-border isn't the exception anymore. It's the default.

Read that again: the hiring model has already gone global. The compliance model hasn't caught up. 

Here's the pattern we keep seeing:

TA builds a beautiful funnel. Sourcing, screening, offer, onboarding - all optimized, all instrumented and all board-approved. 

Then someone tries to hire in Indonesia, Poland or Kenya and the funnel hits a wall no dashboard warned anyone about: local classification rules, statutory notice periods, mandatory benefits, social security enrolment, data residency laws.

And suddenly, "time to hire" isn't a recruitment metric. It's a legal exposure metric. 

The uncomfortable truth: Compliance isn't a blocker to a good TA strategy. It IS the TA strategy, the moment you cross a border. 

If your talent roadmap doesn't have statutory, country-specific regulation baked into the business case (not bolted on after the offer letter), it isn't board-ready. It's a liability with a nice UI.

3 questions every CHRO should be able to answer before the next board meeting:
- Do we know country-by-country, where our classification exposure actually sits?
- Is compliance sitting in the room when we build hiring plans or is it the team we call after something breaks?
- Can we prove (not assume) that our global hiring model would survive an audit today?

Technology gets you candidates. Compliance gets you a business that's still standing in five years.

posts.title: I am delighted to announce my completion of the "AI, Social Media, and the Law" MOOC with the Law Society of Ireland.
posts.author: Mary-Kate McInnes
posts.snippet:
I am delighted to announce my completion of the "AI, Social Media, and the Law" MOOC with the Law Society of Ireland.

To me, this course was a masterclass in how tech regulation is rapidly moving from reacting to digital harm after the fact to proactively embedding platform safety and user choice from the very beginning. Unpacking the emerging Digital Fairness Agenda through these modules showed me how frameworks like the upcoming Digital Fairness Act will mandate "Fairness by Design." As this course highlighted, we are finally moving past the outdated legal fiction of the "perfectly rational consumer" to require built-in protections directly in default interfaces and subscription flows. 

Connecting these high-level regulatory theories to the daily operational risks of businesses using social media and AI as e-commerce tools was extremely interesting for me. Studying Maureen Daly’s insights completely reframed how I view generative AI. Due to the massive grey areas in IP ownership, keeping a "human in the loop!" is an active compliance necessity to prevent copyright infringement. Similarly, exploring influencer marketing with Hazel McDwyer under the Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000 showed me that because influencers are independent contractors, they legally own their content by default. Without strategic contracts, brands can easily pay for a campaign they don't even legally own, all while platforms automatically gain broad licenses to their uploaded IP. 

The course also showed me the major wake-up call needed regarding the borderless security threats that underpin all this digital growth. Learning from Aisling K. about the era of "Agentic liability" and the fact that digital jurisdiction is no longer territorial made me appreciate that when a company handles digital data, their legal exposure is immediate and global. It was fascinating to see how the global legal landscape is scrambling to keep pace, as illustrated by the Council of Europe's technical report showing that 97% of UN Member States have now undertaken or initiated cybercrime and electronic evidence legislative reforms, with 85% of countries using the Budapest Convention as their baseline guideline.

A massive thank you to the Law Society of Ireland and the brilliant experts who guided us through these complex legal landscapes. I’m looking forward to seeing how these compliance insights are applied as we legislate our future!

posts.title: Four years ago, I made one of the most important presentations of my life.
posts.author: Cecilia Serwaa Beremah
posts.snippet:
Four years ago, I made one of the most important presentations of my life.

On the other end of the call was my sister and guardian,Zipporah Osei . 

With borrowed confidence and trembling hands, I tried to convince her that ICT was a good choice after all.

The funny thing is…

I wasn’t even sure I believed what I was saying.

You see, I was one of those children whose entire life was built around one dream:

“I’m going to be a lawyer.”

That was the plan.

Then life took a different turn.

I didn’t get into law school, and after seeing my sister build a career in technology, I decided to pursue a degree in ICT instead.

Looking back today, I realize God wasn’t changing my destination—He was expanding it.

This journey has transformed me in ways I never imagined.

It taught me to lead.

In Level 200, I was entrusted with a leadership position as General Secretary of the GIMPA Association of Technology Students (GATS).

In Level 300, I pioneered the WITE Summit 2025, driven by one realization: many female students in technology struggle with a sense of belonging.

We created a space where women in tech could share their journeys, mentor us, and remind us that we belonged in the room.

To Cyril Tsribi Odonkor  and Kelvin Quartey , our SRC President at the time, thank you for every phone call you made, every door you helped open, and every string you pulled to make that vision a reality.

In my final year, while preparing for my final exams and project defence, I was invited by Glitz Africa HQ   to support the planning and coordination of their first Tech Panel and FinTech & AI Masterclass at the Ghana Female CEOs Summit.

That opportunity reminded me that the seeds you plant quietly often become the opportunities you never expected.

Last month, I graduated with a Bachelor of Science in ICT.

When I think back to the girl who once sat in church crying because she thought not studying Law meant she had failed, I can only smile.

God knew what He was doing all along.

To my family, friends, lecturers, mentors, and everyone who believed in me before I fully believed in myself—thank you.

And above all, thank You, God.

Thank You for ordering my steps, lifting my head, and proving that sometimes the path we never planned becomes the one that reveals our purpose.

Here’s to the next chapter. ❤️
